title: Silence (Avot 1:17)
hookLine: Simeon: I found nothing better for a person than silence
last: SOMEONE ELSE'S SHARE WAS IN THE PILE.

cards: The family dinner where everybody talks at once, every sentence louder than the one before, and nobody really listening.

At the end of the table, one person says almost nothing, until, near the end, one quiet sentence that everybody remembers. Today's sage grew up in rooms like that: rooms full of sages, arguing over Torah.
After a whole life among them, he reported that the best thing he found wasn't a speech.

teach.b: He's Simeon, the son of Rabban Gamaliel from yesterday, raised in the house of the leaders of the sages, surrounded by debate.

His saying: all my days I grew up among the sages, and I found nothing better for a person than silence. The Hebrew says for the body, as if silence were good for you the way sleep is. Then two more lines.
Study isn't the main thing; doing is. And whoever talks too much brings on sin. That last line sounds like an old proverb, and it is.
Proverbs says something close: where words pile up, wrongdoing is never far away. Pile up enough words and something false, cruel or careless slips in.

teach.h: A WORD IS ONE COIN, SILENCE TWO.
teach.b: The Talmud puts a price tag on it: a word is worth one coin, silence is worth two.
And much later in Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Akiva gives the line we're carrying today: a fence around wisdom is silence.
Remember the fence around the Torah, from the start of the tractate? A fence doesn't hide what's inside. It protects it.

Silence keeps what you know from spilling out carelessly, and leaves room for what you don't know yet to come in. This isn't a rule against speaking. Simeon's own teachers spent their lives talking about Torah.
It's about the weight of words: fewer of them, chosen well, and followed by doing.

how: Jewish tradition treats guarding speech (shemirat halashon) as a serious practice, and some Jews take on periods of deliberate silence, especially during times of reflection.

o: a vow to stop speaking for a set number of days
keeping words few, so the ones you say are chosen well
never speaking up, even when something is wrong

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.

s: Simeon said study is the main thing
he said the main thing is doing, not only study.
the Hebrew says silence is good for the body
he found nothing better for the body, for a person, than silence.
a fence around wisdom is silence comes from Rabbi Akiva
it appears later in Pirkei Avot, in chapter three.

games.q: you grew up among the sages, surrounded by debate. someone asks what you learned from them. what do you say?
o: nothing is better for a person than silence.
that study is all that matters.
games.why: Simeon said he found nothing better than silence, and that doing, not only study, is the main thing.

practice: Two minutes of real silence: no words, not even in your head, if you can manage it. When a sentence starts forming, a reply, a plan, an argument, notice it and let it go unsaid.
Listen instead, to the room, to your breath, to whatever's under the noise; you don't have to fill the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Silence. Shetikah in Hebrew. Simeon found nothing better for a person, and Rabbi Akiva called it a fence around wisdom.

orig.note: Hebrew: silence, the fence around wisdom.

carryVoice: Your line: silence is a fence. Not a wall, a fence, around what you know. Until tomorrow.
